placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the north face of blk_randolph_dearborn, the block's Randolph Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its west wall is fixed by the west end of the run's own frontage, 1.5 m clear of the side lot line at that end. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at Randolph Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

persons.name: L. W. Montgomery
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'L. W. MONTGOME' and 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' and 'L. W. MONTGOMERY.' and 'MON TOOMERY.' and 'W. MONTGOMERY.' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 17 December 1833, column 3; the Democrat of 28 January 1834, column 8; the Democrat of 25 March 1834, column 9; the Democrat of 8 April 1834, column 7; the Democrat of 21 May 1834, column 4; the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 13, and 1 further mention(s). The corpus associates the name with Chicago, P. Cohen's store, South Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `shoemaker` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “MONTGOMERY LOTON WM”, “MONTGOMERY LOTON W”, 1835-06-27 to 1835-11-24: 2 federal land entries — E2SE sec 22 T38N R14E; NW sec 23 T38N R14E, 240.00 acres stated in all, for $300.00 (ls0640, ls0646). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: MONTGOMERY LOTON WM matches L. W. Montgomery: the forename names L. W. Montgomery of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees as an initial only. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Montgomery, L. W.” (poll_1834_074, line 243); Poll list of 1835 — “Montgomery, L. W.” (poll_1835_048, line 335). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Montgomery' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Montgomery, Mrs. Laura A. | . Letter. | January 3, 1851. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0735, printed page 195), admitted 1851-01-03 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Montgomery' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins L. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

persons.name: Aaron Russell
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'Aapon Ruseell,' and 'Aaron Rusascll' and 'Aaron Russell' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 29 October 1834, column 6; the Democrat of 12 November 1834, column 11; the Democrat of 3 September 1834, column 12. The corpus associates the name with Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `bookseller` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Aaron Russell as a bookseller at Chicago 3 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: George H Walker
persons.note: THE LADDER'S OWN READING OF THIS EVIDENCE. Read from muster_1832, newspaper_letter_list. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1c), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. muster_1832 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1832 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “WALKER G H”, “WALKER GEORGE H”, 1836-06-22: 2 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 37 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL37CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 37 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL37CHIOT, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $9650.00 (ls1526, ls1527). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $9650.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: WALKER G H matches George H Walker: the forename names George H Walker of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees as an initial only. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

frontage.why: T-0105, the succession T-0079 owes: the core density standard applied to the next core block standing below the bar. THE FACE IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, by the command T-A14 made of it — tools/measure_street_frontage.py randolph washington market franklin — and on the committed dataset Randolph carries 7 documented records and 7 inferred households against Washington's 1 and 0. Randolph is this block's business face by the town's own record, so the block's one free lot on that face takes the row and both free lots on Washington stay open. THE END RULE IS T-A11'S, READ ON THIS BLOCK: this is the easternmost block the plat module reaches on the Randolph tier, so the town-centre end of its frontage is the WEST one, toward Dearborn Street and the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835 — and the row is graded that way, a storey and a half at the west end, a one-room frame cottage in the middle, and an older log cabin at the east. NO COORDINATE IS AUTHORED: the line, its bearing, the lot's own stretch of it and the end the run packs away from are all read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and the 1.5 m setback is the plat module's own lot margin rather than a measurement of this frontage. Lot 4 is an interior lot and not a corner one, so the standard's third clause — a corner lot builds to the corner — has nothing to bind here; the run stands off both of its own side lines by that same margin.
